pos: n. (Peter Abelard, 1079–1142, French dialectician and theologian, author of Sic et Non, twice condemned, and the originator of the moral-influence view of the atonement)
biblical_def: Peter Abelard was the most brilliant and least governable mind of the twelfth century. He humbled his own masters in debate, drew students to Paris by the thousand, and in Sic et Non set contradictory patristic citations side by side without resolving them — a method that taught the schools to examine authority rather than merely recite it, and which did real service to theology. His private life ruined him: the affair with Heloise, her uncle's revenge, the monastery. His doctrine ruined him twice more. Condemned at Soissons in 1121 over his treatise on the Trinity and at Sens in 1141 at Bernard of Clairvaux's prosecution, he died on his way to appeal at Rome. His lasting error is the account of the cross. Abelard taught that Christ's death works upon us by the example of love it displays, kindling love in return, and he denied that any ransom was paid to the Father or any penalty borne. Isa 53:5 forecloses it: “he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities.” Rom 3:25 names Him “a propitiation through faith in his blood,” and Gal 3:13 says He was “made a curse for us.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines atonement as the expiation of sin made by the obedience and personal sufferings of Christ; and propitiation as the atonement or offering which procures forgiveness.
webster_full: ATONE'MENT, n. Agreement; concord; reconciliation, after enmity or controversy.
2. Expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury, or by doing or suffering that which is received in satisfaction for an offense.
The sufferings of Christ are the atonement for the sins of men.
scriptures: Isa 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
Rom 3:25
Whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past, through the forbearance of God;
Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed.
Gal 3:13
Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:
corruption_summary: The moral-influence theory is Abelard's, and it is the most popular account of the cross now preached in the English-speaking world.
corruption_paragraphs: Abelard's view has outlived his condemnation and become the ordinary preaching of liberal Protestantism and a great deal of evangelicalism besides: the cross shows how much God loves us, and the showing is the saving. The display is real — Scripture does commend the love of the cross — but it is a consequence of the atonement and not the atonement itself. If no penalty was borne, the demonstration demonstrates nothing, for a death that accomplishes nothing proves no love. “Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree” (1Pe 2:24) is a transaction, and the stripes heal because the sins were borne.

The deeper corruption is what the theory does to God. Penal substitution holds that God is just and must punish sin, and that in Christ He punished it in a Substitute of His own providing; the moral-influence account quietly concludes that no punishment was necessary, which means sin did not require it, which means the law was not serious. Abelard thought he was defending God against the crude notion of a ransom paid to the devil, and that notion did need correcting; Anselm had already corrected it by directing the satisfaction to God Himself. The recovery is Anselm's question answered with Scripture's own language of propitiation, curse-bearing and imputed righteousness.

pos: n. (Hugh of St Victor, c. 1096–1141, canon regular of the abbey of St Victor in Paris, author of On the Sacraments of the Christian Faith and the founder of Victorine theology)
etymology: Germanic Hugo, mind or spirit; the abbey of St Victor stood outside the walls of Paris.
biblical_def: Hugh of St Victor taught at an abbey school that refused the choice its century was offering between dialectic and devotion. He wrote a full systematic theology, the De Sacramentis, in which the whole history of redemption is ordered under the works of creation and the works of restoration; and he wrote the Didascalicon, the best medieval guide to study. His exegetical rule is the one that matters most to a Protestant reader: the literal and historical sense is the foundation, and no allegory may be built except upon it. He compares the interpreter to a builder who must lay a footing before raising walls, which is the figure of 1Co 3:11, “other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ,” and of Eph 2:20, the house “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets.” Against the fashion for finding mysteries in syllables he insisted that a man learn grammar, geography and history first. His doctrine of the sacraments carries the medieval error of grace conveyed by the sign itself, and his mysticism goes beyond the text. But Psa 119:130 is his instinct: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the literal sense as that which is according to the letter; primitive; real; not figurative or metaphorical.
webster_full: LIT'ERAL, a. According to the letter; primitive; real; not figurative or metaphorical; as, the literal meaning of a phrase.
FOUNDA'TION, n. The basis of an edifice; that part of a building which lies on the ground.
2. The act of fixing the basis; that on which any thing stands, and by which it is supported.
scriptures: For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
Eph 2:20
And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple.
corruption_summary: Hugh laid down that no allegory may stand without a literal footing, and the schools that honoured him went on building without one.
corruption_paragraphs: The medieval fourfold sense was not in itself the problem; the problem was the higher senses floating free of the letter, so that a text could be made to prove whatever the preacher needed. Hugh's rule is the cure, and it is the Reformers' rule after him: establish what the words say in their place and time, and let any further sense be one the Scriptures themselves draw. His own century largely ignored him, and by the fifteenth the allegorical method was the chief engine by which doctrines absent from Scripture were found in it.

The nearer corruption is the modern devotional reading that treats the text as a mirror for the reader's feelings — what this verse means to me — which is allegory with the self in the place of the mystery. 2Ti 3:15 says the holy scriptures “are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus,” which fixes both the subject and the end. The recovery is Hugh's discipline joined to his reverence: learn the letter as a workman learns a footing, and expect the light he expected from it.
roots_summary: Greek themelios (G2310), a foundation; Hebrew pethach (H6608), an opening, entrance; Greek sophizo (G4679), to make wise.

“The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130) — what he expected of the letter.

pos: n. (Richard of St Victor, d. 1173, Scottish-born prior of St Victor in Paris, author of De Trinitate, who argued the plurality of Persons from the nature of perfect love)
etymology: Germanic Ricohard, strong in rule; he is called Scotus in some manuscripts, probably meaning Scottish.
biblical_def: Richard of St Victor succeeded to Hugh's school and is remembered for one argument of real power. In De Trinitate he reasons that the highest good must be the highest love; that love in its perfection cannot be solitary, since to love only oneself is not charity but its opposite; that perfect love therefore requires another to be loved as fully as oneself; and that the highest charity goes further, willing that the beloved be loved by a third, so that there is a co-beloved. From this he concludes that the one God subsists in three. The argument is not a proof from bare reason — Richard works from Scripture's own statement, “God is love” (1Jn 4:8) — but it illuminates the revealed doctrine beautifully. Joh 17:24 gives the eternal loving: “for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world.” Joh 1:18 gives the eternal relation, the only begotten Son “which is in the bosom of the Father.” His mystical writings on contemplation, the Benjamin Minor and Major, are more speculative and go past what the text will bear.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines charity, in a theological sense, as supreme love to God and universal good will to men; and love as that strong affection which arises from a view of excellence.
webster_full: CHAR'ITY, n. In a general sense, love, benevolence, good will.
2. In theology, charity comprehends supreme love to God, and universal good will to men.
LOVE, n. An affection of the mind excited by beauty and worth of any kind, or by the qualities of an object which communicate pleasure.
scriptures: He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love.
Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am; that they may behold my glory, which thou hast given me: for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world.
Joh 1:18
No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.
Pro 8:30
Then I was by him, as one brought up with him: and I was daily his delight, rejoicing always before him;
corruption_summary: Richard's argument is a lamp held to a revealed doctrine, and it becomes an error the moment it is treated as the ground of the doctrine instead.
corruption_paragraphs: The Victorine argument is legitimate as illustration and illegitimate as foundation. We know God is triune because He has revealed it, not because we have deduced that love requires company; and the moment the deduction becomes the ground, the doctrine is at the mercy of the next philosopher's account of love. Modern social-Trinitarian theology makes exactly that move, deriving the Persons from relationality and then deriving ethics and politics from the Persons — a programme that quietly loses divine simplicity and ends with three centres of consciousness in a committee. Richard did not intend it; his reasoning is often cited in its service.

The guard is the classical doctrine the Reformed scholastics kept: one simple divine essence, three Persons distinguished by eternal relations of origin, not by separate wills or separate loves. Pro 8:30 shows Wisdom “daily his delight, rejoicing always before him,” and Joh 17:24 shows the Father loving the Son before the world was. That is the eternal love Richard was reaching for, and it is given, not inferred. Use his lamp and stand on the revelation.
roots_summary: Greek agape (G26), love, charity; monogenes (G3439), only begotten; kolpos (G2859), the bosom.
roots_lines: Greek agape (G26) — love, charity; 1 John 4:8.
Greek monogenes (G3439) — only begotten, unique; John 1:18.
Greek kolpos (G2859) — the bosom, the lap; John 1:18.
Greek agapao (G25) — to love; John 17:24.
Hebrew shaashuim (H8191) — delight; Proverbs 8:30.
usage: “God is love” (1Jn 4:8) — the revealed premise of his argument.
“for thou lovedst me before the foundation of the world” (Joh 17:24) — the eternal loving.
“which is in the bosom of the Father” (Joh 1:18) — the eternal relation.

pos: n. (Alexander of Hales, c. 1185–1245, English Franciscan, first of his order to hold a chair at Paris, under whose name the Summa Halensis was produced)
etymology: Greek Alexandros, defender of men; Hales Owen in Shropshire, his birthplace.
biblical_def: Alexander of Hales was an established Paris master when, near fifty, he entered the Franciscan order and carried his chair with him, making the Franciscans a power in the schools. He fixed the method of the next three centuries by taking Peter Lombard's Sentences as the textbook on which every bachelor must lecture, so that theology was henceforth taught as commentary on a topical arrangement. The great Summa issued under his name was largely the work of his school. Its lasting contribution to Roman doctrine is the developed notion of a treasury of merit — the superabundant satisfactions of Christ and the saints, held by the church and applicable to others, which is the theory indulgences would later require. Scripture does not permit it. “Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt” (Rom 4:4) divides merit from grace absolutely; and “works of righteousness which we have done” (Tit 3:5) are expressly excluded. The Lord Himself leaves no surplus to bank: “We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do” (Luk 17:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines merit as desert; goodness or excellence which entitles one to honor or reward; and supererogation as the performance of more than duty requires.
webster_full: MER'IT, n. Desert; goodness or excellence which entitles one to honor or reward.
2. Value; excellence; worth.
SUPEREROGA'TION, n. The act of doing more than duty requires; performance of more than is required.
scriptures: Rom 4:4
Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt.
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Tit 3:5
Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;
So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.
corruption_summary: The treasury of merits is the bank on which indulgences were drawn, and the account was opened in the schools before it was ever sold at a church door.
corruption_paragraphs: The doctrine requires two things Scripture denies: that a creature may do more than is owed, and that the surplus may be transferred by ecclesiastical act. Luk 17:10 destroys the first, for a servant who has done everything commanded has still only done his duty and has nothing over. Rom 4:4 destroys the second, since what is reckoned of debt is by definition not of grace, and a system that distributes merit is distributing wages. By 1517 the theory had become a trade, and Luther's theses were an attack on a construction the thirteenth-century schools had built.

A related and still common corruption is the devotional version that keeps the structure without the vocabulary — the believer who hopes his extra devotions will count, or that a hard season has earned him something. Eph 2:9 answers it in five words: “Not of works, lest any man should boast.” The recovery is the imputed righteousness of Christ, which is not a quantity held by the church and dispensed, but His own obedience reckoned to the believer who trusts Him, whole and immediately and without remainder.
roots_summary: Greek opheilema (G3783), that which is owed, a debt; achreios (G888), unprofitable; kauchaomai (G2744), to boast.
roots_lines: Greek misthos (G3408) — wages, reward; Romans 4:4.
Greek opheilema (G3783) — a debt, that which is due; Romans 4:4.
Greek kauchaomai (G2744) — to boast, to glory; Ephesians 2:9.
Greek achreios (G888) — unprofitable, useless; Luke 17:10.
Greek palingenesia (G3824) — regeneration; Titus 3:5.
usage: “to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt” (Rom 4:4) — merit and grace divided.
“Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9) — against a transferable surplus.
“We are unprofitable servants” (Luk 17:10) — no treasury to draw on.

pos: n. (Albertus Magnus, c. 1200–1280, Dominican bishop and universal doctor, who naturalized Aristotle in the Latin West and taught Thomas Aquinas)
etymology: Germanic Adalbert, noble and bright; Magnus, the great, a title given in his lifetime.
biblical_def: Albertus Magnus set himself to make the whole of Aristotle intelligible to Latin readers, paraphrasing and commenting on every work then available, and he did it at a time when Aristotle's physics and metaphysics were under suspicion at Paris. He was also a genuine naturalist who dissected, observed and corrected his authorities from what he saw, writing on plants, minerals and animals with a care rare before the seventeenth century. His pupil was Thomas Aquinas, and he defended his pupil's work after his death. The theological warrant for such study is Rom 1:20, that “the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made,” and Psa 19:1, “The heavens declare the glory of God.” Col 1:17 keeps the creature in its place: “he is before all things, and by him all things consist.” The danger in his achievement was the one his century felt: a pagan philosopher's categories, received wholesale, began to set the terms in which revelation was discussed, and that inversion is the burden the Reformation had to lift.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines natural philosophy as the science of material natural bodies, of their properties, powers and motions; and nature as the system of created things.
webster_full: NAT'URAL PHILOS'OPHY, the science of material natural bodies, of their properties, powers and motions.
NA'TURE, n. In a general sense, whatever is made or produced; a word that comprehends all the works of God.
The established course of things; the regular course of events.
scriptures: Psa 19:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
Rom 1:20
For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:
Col 1:17
And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.
Job 38:4
Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.
corruption_summary: Albert proved that the study of the creature is a Christian calling, and his century proved how quickly the philosopher's categories start dictating to Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: There is no Reformed objection to natural science; Rom 1:20 and Psa 19:1 establish that the works of God declare Him, and a man who dissects a plant to see how God made it is engaged in lawful and worshipful work. The corruption is the reversal, in which the system borrowed to describe nature becomes the frame revelation must fit. Aristotle's eternal world, his unmoved mover who does not know particulars, and his account of the soul all required adjustment, and the schools spent two centuries adjusting them — sometimes by adjusting Scripture. Job 38:4 is God's own question to the natural philosopher: “Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?”

The modern form of the same corruption is the opposite reflex: a Christian suspicion of natural study as such, as though attention to the creature were a rival to attention to the Creator. That is not the Reformed position either. General revelation is real revelation, insufficient for salvation and sufficient to leave men “without excuse” (Rom 1:20). The recovery is Albert's diligence under Scripture's authority: observe the world honestly, and let no philosophy — ancient or current — hold a veto over what God has said.

Hebrew raqia (H7549) — the firmament, expanse; Psalm 19:1.
Greek poiema (G4161) — that which is made, a work; Romans 1:20.
Greek anapologetos (G379) — without excuse; Romans 1:20.
Greek sunistemi (G4921) — to hold together, to consist; Colossians 1:17.

“being understood by the things that are made” (Rom 1:20) — general revelation, really given.
“Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 38:4) — the philosopher put in his place.

pos: n. (Bonaventure, 1221–1274, Italian Franciscan, minister general of his order, cardinal-bishop of Albano, called the Seraphic Doctor; author of the Journey of the Mind to God)
etymology: Italian Bonaventura, good fortune, good coming; his baptismal name was Giovanni di Fidanza.
biblical_def: Bonaventure governed the Franciscans through their worst internal crisis and wrote the order's official life of Francis, ordering the destruction of the earlier ones. As a theologian he is the counterpart of Aquinas: where Thomas orders knowledge, Bonaventure orders ascent, and his Itinerarium Mentis in Deum traces the mind's journey from the creature through the image to the God above both. Its best pages are a genuinely Christian longing, and Psa 73:25 is their motto: “Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.” Php 3:8 is the same instinct in Paul, counting all things “but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord.” Two errors run through him. The ascent is structured so that contemplation reaches a region beyond the Word, where the soul passes over in a darkness that Scripture does not describe; and his Marian devotion is extravagant even by thirteenth-century measure, addressing to Mary offices and titles that belong to Christ. Col 2:9 is the correction: “For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines contemplation as the act of the mind in considering with attention; meditation; study; and in a religious sense, holy meditation.
webster_full: CONTEMPLA'TION, n. The act of the mind in considering with attention; meditation; study; continued attention of the mind to a particular subject.
2. Holy meditation; attention to sacred things.
MYS'TICISM, n. Obscurity of doctrine. 2. The doctrine of the Mystics, who profess a pure, sublime and perfect devotion.
scriptures: Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.
Php 3:8

Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,
Joh 14:6
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
Col 2:9
For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
corruption_summary: Bonaventure's ladder of ascent ends above the Word, and a devotion that climbs past Scripture always arrives somewhere Scripture did not send it.
corruption_paragraphs: Mystical theology of this kind concedes in principle that the highest knowledge of God is not mediated by His Word, and the concession is fatal however devout the climber. Joh 14:6 fixes the only way — “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” — and Christ is known in the Scriptures and nowhere else with certainty. Where the ladder goes beyond the text it goes beyond warrant, and what is found there cannot be tested. The Reformed tradition is not against communion with God; it insists that communion runs through Word, sacrament and prayer, which are the means He appointed.

The second corruption is the Marian piety, which in Bonaventure and the works long attributed to him reaches the point of calling Mary the neck through which all grace flows, and of transferring psalms addressed to the LORD to her. This is not excess of affection but a redirection of worship, and it is the ground on which Rome's later Marian definitions were built. Col 2:9 leaves no deficit for a mediatrix to supply: the fulness of the Godhead dwells in Christ bodily. The recovery is to keep Bonaventure's longing for God and to seek its satisfaction where he looked past — in the written Word and the one Mediator.
roots_summary: Greek pleroma (G4138), fulness; gnosis (G1108), knowledge; Hebrew chaphets (H2654), to desire, to delight in.
roots_lines: Greek pleroma (G4138) — fulness, completeness; Colossians 2:9.
Greek theotes (G2320) — Godhead, deity; Colossians 2:9.
Greek huperecho (G5242) — to surpass, excellency; Philippians 3:8.
Greek hodos (G3598) — a way, a road; John 14:6.
Hebrew chaphets (H2654) — to desire, to delight in; Psalm 73:25.
usage: “Whom have I in heaven but thee?” (Psa 73:25) — the longing that is sound in him.
“no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6) — the limit his ladder passed.
“For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9) — against a mediatrix.

pos: n. (John Duns Scotus, c. 1266–1308, Scottish Franciscan, called the Subtle Doctor, author of the Ordinatio and the chief advocate of the immaculate conception of Mary)
etymology: From Duns in Berwickshire; Scotus, the Scot. The English word dunce comes from the later humanist contempt for his followers.
biblical_def: Duns Scotus is the hardest of the great scholastics to read and among the most original. Against Aquinas he held that being is predicated univocally of God and the creature, so that the word means the same thing in both uses though infinitely differently realized; he grounded the individuality of each thing in its own haecceitas, its thisness; and he gave the divine will a priority over the divine intellect that makes God's free decree, not the nature of things, the reason the moral order is what it is. Reformed theology has drawn on him more than it usually admits, particularly on the primacy of the will and the contingency of the created order. His great error is Marian. He proposed the distinction that made the immaculate conception defensible: Mary was redeemed by Christ too, but preserved from original sin rather than cleansed of it, which he called a more perfect redemption. Scripture allows no exception. “For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Rom 3:23); Mary herself says “my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour” (Luk 1:47); and 1Jn 1:8 warns those who say they have no sin.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines subtilty as refinement; extreme acuteness; and the Immaculate Conception as the Romish doctrine that the Virgin was conceived without original sin.
webster_full: SUBTILTY, n. Thinness; fineness; exility; as the subtilty of air.
2. Refinement; extreme acuteness; as the subtilty of arguments.
IMMAC'ULATE, a. Spotless; pure; unstained; undefiled; without blemish.
scriptures: Rom 3:23
For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;
Luk 1:47
And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour.
Gal 4:4
But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law,
If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
corruption_summary: Scotus invented the distinction that made the immaculate conception thinkable, and Rome defined it as dogma five and a half centuries later.
corruption_paragraphs: The objection in Scotus's day was unanswerable on its face: if Mary never had original sin, Christ is not her Saviour, and Luk 1:47 has her confessing that He is. Scotus answered that preservation from a debt is a greater benefit than release from it, so Mary was redeemed more perfectly, not less. It is ingenious and it is not exegesis. Rom 3:23 says “all have sinned” without a carve-out, Gal 4:4 says the Son was “made of a woman, made under the law” and says nothing of an immaculate one, and the whole argument stands on a theological convenience rather than on a text. Pius IX defined it in 1854 on this basis.

The second matter is a caution rather than a corruption. Scotus's voluntarism — the priority of God's will — is congenial to Reformed theology and can be pressed too far, into the claim that God could have commanded the contrary of the moral law, which would make righteousness arbitrary. Scripture holds both that God does “according to his will” without constraint and that He cannot deny Himself. The recovery is the Reformed scholastic balance: the decree is free, and the God who decrees is immutably holy, so that the law reflects His nature and His sovereign appointment at once.
roots_summary: Greek hustereo (G5302), to come short; soter (G4990), Saviour; ginomai (G1096), to be made or born.
roots_lines: Greek hamartano (G264) — to sin, to miss the mark; Romans 3:23.
Greek hustereo (G5302) — to come short, to fall behind; Romans 3:23.
Greek soter (G4990) — Saviour; Luke 1:47.
Greek ginomai (G1096) — to become, to be made; Galatians 4:4.
Greek planao (G4105) — to deceive, to lead astray; 1 John 1:8.
usage: “For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Rom 3:23) — no exception granted.
“my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour” (Luk 1:47) — Mary confessing her need.
“made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal 4:4) — the incarnation without an immaculate mother.

pos: n. (William of Ockham, c. 1287–1347, English Franciscan, the greatest of the nominalists, whose via moderna shaped the schools in which Luther was trained)
etymology: From Ockham in Surrey; the maxim called Ockham's razor — that explanations should not multiply entities needlessly — is named for him.
biblical_def: William of Ockham denied that universals have any existence outside the mind: only individuals are real, and a general term is a sign standing for many singulars. From this he drew consequences that ran through the late Middle Ages. Knowledge of God by natural reason is far weaker than Aquinas allowed, so revelation must carry more weight — a conclusion with a Protestant flavour. God's will is not bound by any order of natures, so what is right is right because He wills it, and He could by His absolute power do otherwise than He has ordained. He also fought a long political battle against Pope John XXII over apostolic poverty and papal authority, was excommunicated, and wrote in defence of the empire against papal claims. The doctrine of God he bequeathed has a true centre: Eph 1:11 says God “worketh all things after the counsel of his own will,” and Psa 115:3 that “he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased.” Isa 46:10 and Dan 4:35 say the same. What his school added was a doctrine of justification in which man, by doing what is in him, disposes himself for grace — the very scheme the young Luther was taught and later repudiated.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the nominalists as a sect of school philosophers, the followers of Ockham, who maintained that universals have no real existence, but are mere names or words.
webster_full: NOM'INALIST, n. One of a sect of school philosophers, the followers of Occam or Ockham, who maintained that universals have no real existence, but are mere names or words.
SOV'EREIGNTY, n. Supreme power; supremacy; the possession of the highest power, or of uncontrollable power.
WILL, n. Choice; determination; the faculty by which we determine either to do or forbear.
scriptures: Eph 1:11
In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:
But our God is in the heavens: he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased.
Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:
Dan 4:35

And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?
corruption_summary: Ockham's school taught that a man who does what lies in him will be given grace, and that sentence is the one Luther had to be delivered from.
corruption_paragraphs: The late nominalist formula — facere quod in se est, to do what is in oneself — held that God in His ordained power will not deny grace to the man who does his natural best. It is Semi-Pelagianism with a voluntarist foundation, and it was the working doctrine of the schools at Erfurt where Luther studied. He tried it, and found that a conscience which takes the law seriously can never know whether it has done its best; the terror of that uncertainty drove him to Rom 1:17. Tit 3:5 and Rom 4:4 had already settled it: grace that answers a man's best effort is wages, not grace.

The second caution concerns the razor and its modern use. As a rule for framing explanations it is sound and still serviceable. As a metaphysical principle it was pressed into a denial that natural reason can establish much about God at all, and the long effect was to divide faith from knowledge — a separation the modern mind inherited and widened, so that doctrine is now commonly treated as a value rather than a truth claim. The Reformed answer keeps both: God's sovereign will is absolutely free, Eph 1:11 is a statement of fact, and what He has revealed is knowledge.

“he hath done whatsoever he hath pleased” (Psa 115:3) — sovereignty without constraint.
“My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure” (Isa 46:10) — the decree that does not fail.

pos: n. (Marsilius of Padua, c. 1275–1342, Italian physician and political theorist, author of Defensor Pacis, which denied the papacy any coercive jurisdiction whatever)
etymology: Italian Marsilio, from Latin Marsilius; Padua in the Veneto, where he was born and trained.
biblical_def: Marsilius of Padua wrote the most radical political book of the Middle Ages. The Defensor Pacis of 1324 argues that all coercive authority belongs to the civil community and its chosen legislator; that the church has no coercive power at all, only the ministry of word and sacrament; that the clergy are subject to the magistrate in all civil matters; that a general council, summoned by the civil authority and composed of clergy and laity, is the church's highest voice; and that the papal plenitude of power is a usurpation with no foundation in Scripture. He was excommunicated and took refuge with the Emperor Louis of Bavaria. On the central negation he is right, and the texts are his. “My kingdom is not of this world” (Joh 18:36) denies the church a sword; “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” (2Co 10:4) says the same of its means; and the Lord's own order in Luk 22:26, that the chief shall be “as he that doth serve,” is the standing rebuke of a hierarchy that exercises dominion.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines jurisdiction as the legal power of judging and determining; and Erastianism, in church history, as the doctrine that the church is subject to the civil power.
webster_full: JURISDIC'TION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing the laws and distributing justice.
2. Power of governing or legislating.
3. The limit within which power may be exercised.
scriptures: Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve.
But Jesus called them unto him, and said, Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
corruption_summary: Marsilius demolished the papal sword and handed it to the magistrate, which is the error the next three centuries of state churches had to pay for.
corruption_paragraphs: The negation is sound and the replacement is not. Having denied the church coercive power, Marsilius lodged all of it in the civil legislator — including the summoning of councils and the discipline of heretics — and so wrote the charter of Erastianism. That is the arrangement under which the Marian fires burned, the Act of Uniformity ejected two thousand ministers, and Scottish Covenanters were shot on the moors. The 1689 Confession draws the line Marsilius missed: Christ is the only head of His church, the magistrate has no power over the faith or worship of the saints, and the church's discipline is spiritual and belongs to its own officers.

The sphere doctrine is the recovery. Family, church and state are each ordained by God with proper and limited authority, and neither of the latter two may absorb the other. Rome made the church a state; Marsilius made the church a department of the state; Scripture makes it the assembly of Christ's people, governed by elders, wielding no sword and answerable to no magistrate in matters of faith. “Ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them” (Mat 20:25) is said to mark off what the church is not to be, and it marks off equally what the church is not to serve.

pos: n. (Siger of Brabant, c. 1240–c. 1284, master of arts at Paris and chief of the radical Aristotelians, whose theses were condemned in 1270 and 1277)
etymology: Germanic Sigiher, victory-spear; Brabant, the duchy in the Low Countries.
biblical_def: Siger of Brabant taught in the faculty of arts at Paris, and he did what the theologians feared: he expounded Aristotle as Aristotle, and where the Philosopher contradicted the faith he reported the contradiction rather than resolving it. Three theses drew the condemnations of 1270 and 1277 — that the world is eternal and uncreated, that there is one intellect common to all men so that no personal soul survives, and that philosophy may demonstrate what faith denies. Whether Siger actually held the last as a doctrine of double truth is disputed; what is not disputed is that his teaching made the claim available, and that Aquinas wrote against him on the unity of the intellect. Scripture settles each point. “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth” (Gen 1:1) denies an eternal world; Heb 11:3 says the worlds “were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear”; and Joh 17:17, “thy word is truth,” denies that there are two truths which may conflict. Siger was summoned before the inquisitor of France, fled to the papal court, and was killed there by his own secretary.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines truth as conformity to fact or reality; exact accordance with that which is, or has been, or shall be; and creation as the act of creating; the act of causing to exist.
webster_full: TRUTH, n. Conformity to fact or reality; exact accordance with that which is, or has been, or shall be.
2. True state of facts or things.
CREA'TION, n. The act of creating; the act of causing to exist; and especially, the act of bringing this world into existence.
scriptures: Gen 1:1
In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
Heb 11:3
Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear.
Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.
Pro 1:7
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
corruption_summary: The double-truth device lets a man hold one thing as a philosopher and its contrary as a believer, and it is alive and well in every faith-and-science compromise built the same way.
corruption_paragraphs: Whether or not Siger taught it as doctrine, the position attributed to him is the one that matters, because it is perennial: reason reaches one conclusion, faith confesses another, and the two are kept in separate rooms. Joh 17:17 forbids the arrangement, for if God's word is truth then nothing true can contradict it. The modern version is the scholar who teaches in the lecture hall that the world made itself and confesses in church that God made it, and calls the two non-overlapping. That is not humility about the limits of knowledge; it is the surrender of the claim that Scripture tells us what happened.

The eternity of the world and the common intellect are the particular errors, and both are denied flatly. Gen 1:1 gives a beginning, Heb 11:3 gives creation by the word out of nothing, and the whole canon gives each man a soul that will stand in judgment. Pro 1:7 states the order Siger inverted: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.” Aristotle is a useful servant and a ruinous master, and the 1277 condemnation, whatever its heavy-handedness, was defending something true against a method that had made revelation answerable to a pagan physics.
